title: Four Thousand Weeks
author: Oliver Burkeman
blurb: Oliver Burkeman, a former productivity enthusiast, argues that most time management advice rests on an impossible promise: that with enough efficiency, we can finally get on top of everything. The average human life lasts only about four thousand weeks, and no system can make that enough for all our ambitions. Worse, becoming more efficient often just brings more demands. Drawing on philosophy and psychology, Burkeman suggests a different path: accept your limits, make hard choices about what to neglect, and stop treating the present as a mere stepping stone to some future moment of control. He explores why we flee into distraction, why patience is a superpower, why rest needs no justification, and why time is richer when shared with others. The result is a liberating, deeply humane guide to spending a finite life well.

lessons.t: You Only Get Four Thousand Weeks
lessons.b: An average life lasts about four thousand weeks, and facing that limit honestly is the starting point for using time well.
Getting through tasks faster rarely frees you, because doing more usually just attracts more to do, like an inbox that refills as you empty it.
issues: scene 2: A faint, half-transparent rectangle sits at the bottom of the inbox panel, below the seventh row. It looks like an inbox row stuck mid-animation. The 'Inbox zero.' headline and checkmark also stay as low-contrast pale amber ghosts beside the refilled inbox, which reads as unfinished rather than intentional. (fix: Either fully render the eighth row or remove it so nothing is left partly faded. Either remove 'Inbox zero.' and the check once the inbox refills, or show them at full opacity with a clear strike-through to show the state has passed.)

lessons.b: Since you can never do everything, the real skill is deliberately deciding which important things you will fail at so you can focus on what matters most.
issues: scene 1: The bottom row of cards in the 'wall' grid sits on the container's bottom border and looks clipped by it. The grid has no bottom padding, unlike the top. (fix: Make the wall container taller by about 20px, or reduce card height or row gap, so the bottom row has the same inner padding as the top row.)

scene 7: The 'MISSING OUT' drawing (an angular 'h' shape with a dashed circle) does not read as a chair or any recognisable object. The floating grey cards are scattered with no visible link to either figure, so the picture does not clearly show 'stop fighting reality' or 'attention settles'. (fix: Redraw the left figure as a clearly recognisable empty chair or a faded figure looking at drifting cards. Group the grey cards as drifting away from that figure, for example with a few motion lines, so the contrast with the settled amber 'what you picked' reads at a glance.)

lessons.b: Distraction is often an escape from the discomfort of facing hard, limited, uncertain work, so the cure is accepting that discomfort rather than relying only on willpower or apps.
Treating every moment as a means to some future payoff robs you of life now, so value activities like rest and hobbies for their own sake.
issues: scene 8: The large pen drawing runs down over the 'THIS WEEK' label, partly covering it. It also extends to the bottom edge and nearly collides with the visualgrowth.app brand mark. (fix: Shorten the pen and rotate it so its tip ends on the card, above the label. Move the 'THIS WEEK' label clear of the pen, e.g. centred under the card with at least 24px gap. Keep the whole illustration above y≈780 so it stays away from the brand mark.)

lessons.b: Meaningful work and change unfold at their own pace, so staying with something through its slow, unoriginal early stages is what eventually leads somewhere distinctive.
